title: Language Models Need Sleep
hook: Humans consolidate the day's memories while sleeping. This paper gives LLMs a 'sleep' phase to distill fragile short-term context into stable long-term weights — and a 'dreaming' phase to rehearse.
key_points: LLMs are good at in-context learning but can't transfer that temporary knowledge into long-term parameters.
A 'Sleep' paradigm consolidates fragile short-term memories into stable weights via replay.
Memory Consolidation uses 'Knowledge Seeding' — upward distillation from a smaller self into a larger network.
A 'Dreaming' phase uses RL to generate a synthetic-data curriculum, self-improving without human supervision.
content_html: Today's LLMs can pick up new information within a conversation through in-context learning, but that knowledge is fragile — it lives in the context window and vanishes when the session ends. The model never folds it back into its long-term parameters. Borrowing from how humans consolidate memories during sleep, this paper proposes giving models an explicit "sleep" phase to do the same.
extra_html:
How it works

Sleep has two stages. The first, Memory Consolidation, is an upward distillation the authors call Knowledge Seeding: the memories of a "smaller self" are distilled into a larger network, adding capacity while preserving what was learned. Their proof-of-concept is a generalized distillation that combines on-policy distillation with RL-based imitation learning. The second stage, Dreaming, is a self-improvement phase where the model uses reinforcement learning to generate a curriculum of synthetic data, rehearsing new knowledge and refining existing skills without human supervision.

Why it matters

Continual learning — absorbing new knowledge over time without forgetting the old — is one of the open gaps between current LLMs and the way people learn. Framing it as a periodic offline "sleep" that replays and consolidates experience is an evocative way to attack it. The authors report gains on long-horizon, continual-learning, knowledge-incorporation, and few-shot tasks, supporting the idea that models, like us, may benefit from time spent not predicting but consolidating.

related.title: Ring Attention for Near-Infinite Context
related.hook: Spread one long sequence across many devices and compute attention blockwise - the context length you can handle grows with the number of devices, all with exact attention and no extra overhead.

related.title: Extending Context Windows via Positional Interpolation
related.hook: Don't extrapolate to positions the model never saw - squeeze the position indices back inside the trained range, and a short fine-tune stretches the context window many times over.
